title: Randomness for games
sub: A loot table on prefix sums and upper_bound, a fair Fisher–Yates shuffle, System.Random versus UnityEngine.Random and seed determinism
cards/0/title: A loot table: Random Pick with Weight
cards/0/body:
Random Pick with Weight (LeetCode #528). Given an array of weights w, the method PickIndex() returns index i with probability w[i] / sum(w). 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴, weights from 1 to 10⁵, up to 10⁴ calls.

This is the loot table of any game: a sword with weight 1, a potion with weight 3, gold with weight 2 — the potion drops half the time. The same goes for picking an enemy to spawn, an NPC line, a room for a procedural level. “How do you make a weighted drop, and how do you make it fast” is a frequent question at Unity interviews.

There are two naive solutions. Expand the table into an array where index i is repeated w[i] times and pick a random cell — O(1) per pick, but O(sum w) memory, up to 10⁹ cells. Or, for every pick, walk the weights subtracting them from a random number — O(n) per pick, no extra memory.
cards/1/title: Prefix sums of weights and upper_bound
cards/1/body:
Lay the weight segments end to end on a number line: item 0 takes [0, w₀), item 1 takes [w₀, w₀ + w₁), and so on. The right ends are the prefix sums prefix[i] = w[0] + … + w[i]; with weights ≥ 1 they strictly increase. A random r from [0, total) lands in item i’s segment with probability w[i] / total — the segment length over the length of the line.

Which segment r landed in: the first i with prefix[i] > r — that is upper_bound(r) over the prefix array. Building is O(n) once, a pick is O(log n), memory is O(n). The linear walk from the previous card does the same thing, only it finds the segment by scanning.

The boundary is strictly greater. With w = [1, 3, 2] the prefixes are [1, 4, 6]: item 1 owns r = 1, 2, 3, while r = 4 already belongs to item 2. The segments are half-open: the left end is your own, the right end is the neighbour’s. With Array.BinarySearch it is the same: the first prefix > r is the first prefix ≥ r + 1; if found — its index, if not — ~insertion point.
cards/2/q: w = [5, 1, 4], prefix = [5, 6, 10]. rnd.Next(10) returned 6. Which item dropped?
cards/2/explain: The first prefix greater than 6 is 10, index 2. Item 1’s segment is [5, 6), it owns only r = 5; six is the left end of item 2’s segment, [6, 10). If you search for the first prefix ≥ r, every segment shifts by one: item 0 gets r from 0 to 5 — 6 values out of 10 instead of 5 — and item 2 gets 3 instead of 4.
cards/2/wrong/1: That is the answer when searching for the first prefix ≥ r. Item 1’s segment is [5, 6), and 6 is not in it.
cards/2/wrong/2: Item 0 owns r from 0 to 4: its segment is [0, 5).
cards/3/explain: The total weight is the last prefix, and Next(total) gives r from [0, total). A segment with prefix[mid] <= r ended at or before r — the answer is further right: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise prefix[mid] > r, and mid may be the answer: hi = mid. This is the “least i such that prefix[i] > r” template with hi = n − 1: r < total, so the last item always qualifies.
cards/4/title: A loot table in Unity: float and zero weights
cards/4/body:
In Unity weights are often float and live in a ScriptableObject. Build the prefixes once — in OnEnable (and, in the editor, also in OnValidate after the weights are edited), not on every drop: otherwise it is O(n) and a new array per pick.

The float trap. UnityEngine.Random.value and Random.Range(float, float) return a number including both bounds: Random.Range(0f, total) can return exactly total. An upper_bound over the band [0, n) would then return n — past the end of the array. That is why the candidates are [0, n − 1], as in PickIndex: r == total goes to the last item. Random.Range(int, int), on the contrary, excludes the upper bound, like System.Random.Next.

Zero weights. A weight of 0 — an item temporarily disabled — breaks the strict growth of the prefixes: w = [1, 0, 2] → [1, 1, 3]. Your own upper_bound survives this: it looks for the first prefix > r, and a zero-length segment never matches. But Array.BinarySearch with duplicates returns some of the equal ones — for example, the disabled item. One gap remains in the float version: if the last item is disabled, r == total goes to it. The simplest fix is to leave zero-weight items out of the table when building it.
cards/5/q: What is true about a loot table on prefix sums? Select all.
cards/5/options/0: Prefixes are built once, a pick is O(log n)
cards/5/options/1: With zero weights Array.BinarySearch(prefix, r + 1) can return a disabled item
cards/5/options/2: UnityEngine.Random.Range(0f, total) can return exactly total
cards/5/options/3: The sum of 10⁴ weights up to 10⁵ does not fit in int
cards/5/options/4: UnityEngine.Random.Range(0, n) for int can return n
cards/5/explain: The table does not change — prefixes are computed once, then it is only binary search. On w = [1, 0, 2] the prefixes are [1, 1, 3]; with r = 0 we search for 1, the very first midpoint is index 1 with weight 0, and the method returns it. The float version of Range includes both bounds. 10⁴ · 10⁵ = 10⁹ — less than int.MaxValue ≈ 2.1·10⁹. The int version of Range excludes the upper bound.
cards/6/body:
Shuffle an Array (LeetCode #384): a class with Shuffle() — return a random permutation, with all n! equally likely — and Reset() — return the original order.

Fisher–Yates: go from the end; at step i pick j uniformly from [0, i] — including i itself — and swap a[i] and a[j]. After the step the tail [i..n − 1] is final. Why it is fair: the first step has n options, the second n − 1, …, so there are n · (n − 1) · … · 2 = n! equally likely paths, and different paths give different permutations — each with probability exactly 1/n!. O(n) time, in place.

Two classic mistakes. “Swap each element with a random one from all of them”, j = rnd.Next(n): there are nⁿ paths, and nⁿ is not divisible by n! for n ≥ 3. With three elements that is 27 paths for 6 permutations, so some permutations come up with probability 5/27 and others 4/27. The second mistake is j = rnd.Next(i), without i itself: that is Sattolo’s algorithm, it produces only cyclic permutations, and no element ever stays in place.

In a game: a deck of cards, the Tetris piece “bag” (the seven pieces are shuffled and dealt in order, so there are no long droughts of the piece you need), a track queue, the order of waves.
cards/7/q: After this shuffle the deck [A, B, C] only ever comes out as [B, C, A] or [C, A, B]: no card stays in its place. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/7/explain: Next(i) gives j from [0, i − 1]: the element at position i is forced to move. That is Sattolo’s algorithm — on three cards it yields only two cycles out of six permutations. It must be Next(i + 1): j from [0, i], so “staying in place” is also one of the equally likely outcomes.
cards/8/q: The naive shuffle: for i = 0, 1, …, n − 1 swap a[i] with a[rnd.Next(n)]. Why is it uneven on three elements even with a perfect generator?
cards/8/options/0: There are 3³ = 27 paths and 3! = 6 permutations: 27 is not divisible by 6, so they cannot be shared equally
cards/8/options/1: It is uniform: every element took part in a swap with every other
cards/8/options/2: The generator repeats numbers, so some permutations come up more often
cards/8/options/3: The last element never takes part in a swap
cards/8/explain: Each of the 27 paths is equally likely and produces some permutation. For six permutations to come up equally often, each would need 27 / 6 = 4.5 paths — impossible. In fact, starting from [1, 2, 3], the permutations [1, 3, 2], [2, 1, 3] and [2, 3, 1] get 5 paths each, the other three get 4: a 25% skew.
cards/8/wrong/1: “Swapped with everyone” does not mean “all permutations equally”: you have to count paths, and there are 27 of them for 6 outcomes.
cards/8/wrong/2: The question assumes a perfect generator: even if every Next(n) is fair, the paths are not split evenly across permutations.
cards/8/wrong/3: The last element moves too — at step i = n − 1 and, by chance, at other steps. The problem is in the path count.
cards/9/body:
UnityEngine.Random is a static class with one global state. InitState(seed) sets the seed, and the Random.state property lets you save and restore the state; call it from the main thread. Being global is the main problem: any code that also calls Random (effects, AI, a third-party plugin) shifts the sequence, and the loot for the same seed comes out different.

System.Random is an object: every instance has its own state, and new Random(seed) repeats its sequence. But the .NET documentation does not promise that the algorithm stays the same across versions: for saves and networked games a few-line generator of your own (xorshift, PCG) is more reliable. An instance is not thread-safe: concurrent calls from several threads corrupt its state. Random.Shared (.NET 6+) is thread-safe, but Unity does not have it. In .NET Framework a seedless new Random() takes its seed from a timer, and instances created back to back produce the same numbers. In .NET Core and .NET 5+ the default seed is random, and the Mono in current Unity versions takes this class from .NET Core and behaves the same way. Older versions and other platforms promise nothing, though, so the rule is simple: one instance per system, not a new Random() per roll.

Unity.Mathematics.Random is a struct with explicit state for Jobs and Burst; its seed must not be zero.

Seed determinism means the same seed and the same sequence of calls. It is broken by: one generator shared by several systems; calls in Update, whose number depends on FPS; a seed taken from string.GetHashCode() — in .NET Core and .NET 5+ a string hash differs from process to process, and even on Mono the documentation does not promise it is stable; iterating a HashSet or Dictionary — their order is not guaranteed and depends on key hashes and on the history of removals. The roguelike technique is a separate stream per system: map, loot, AI, each with its own seed derived from the world seed.
cards/10/q: A replay must reproduce a fight from its seed. What breaks reproducibility? Select all.
cards/10/options/0: Loot, AI and particles all draw numbers from the same UnityEngine.Random
cards/10/options/1: The crit chance is rolled in Update rather than in a simulation step
cards/10/options/2: The fight seed is the arena name: new System.Random(arenaName.GetHashCode()) on .NET 5+
cards/10/options/3: Loot has its own new System.Random(seed), called only by the loot system
cards/10/options/4: The seed is saved in the replay file together with the player’s input
cards/10/explain: A shared generator: particles depend on graphics settings, and every extra particle shifts loot and AI. Update runs once per frame — at a different FPS there will be a different number of rolls. On .NET 5+ string.GetHashCode() differs in every process — the seed is different on every run. A separate generator per system and the seed in the replay file are exactly what makes it reproducible.
cards/11/q: You are solving Random Pick with Weight out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: are weights integers? Can they be zero? Does the table change? How many picks?
cards/11/items/1: Naive: walk the weights subtracting them from a random number — O(n) per pick
cards/11/items/2: Idea: prefix sums of weights are the right ends of segments on a line; the pick is the first prefix > r
cards/11/items/3: Code: prefixes in the constructor, in PickIndex — r = Next(total) and upper_bound
cards/11/items/5: Complexity: O(n) to build, O(log n) per pick, O(n) memory
cards/11/items/6: Edge cases: one item, zero weights, sum overflow, float with an inclusive bound
cards/11/explain: The r = 4 example sits exactly on a segment boundary: it checks that the search uses “strictly greater”. The question “does the table change?” at the clarification step opens the conversation about the Fenwick tree and the alias method.
cards/12/title: When O(log n) is not enough: aliases and changing weights
cards/12/body:
If there are millions of picks and the table does not change, there is the alias method: O(n) to build and O(1) per pick. The table has n columns of equal height, each holding at most two items: its “own” with share prob[i] and a “neighbour” alias[i]. A pick is a uniform column plus one coin flip inside it.

If weights change between picks (an item ran out, a chance grows with every miss), rebuilding the prefixes costs O(n) per change. A Fenwick tree gives O(log n) for both a weight update and a pick.

In an interview prefixes and upper_bound are enough; aliases and Fenwick are a chance to show you know where to go next.
cards/12/deep:
Building the alias table. Multiply the probabilities by n — the average column becomes exactly 1. Columns below 1 (“small”) are topped up from columns above 1 (“large”): take a small s and a large l, set prob[s] = p[s], alias[s] = l, and subtract the missing 1 − p[s] from l; if l drops below 1, it moves to the small ones. Each step closes one column, so building is O(n). Because of float rounding, whatever columns remain at the end are set to 1.

A Fenwick tree stores partial sums of the weights so that updating one weight and finding “the first prefix greater than r” by descending over the bits of the index are both O(log n). It is the choice for tables that change on every drop.

The modulo is biased. rng() % n is uniform only if the number of possible generator values is divisible by n: with 2³² values and n = 3, remainder 0 comes up for one more value than the others. The skew is tiny, but there is no reason to write the modulo yourself: Next(n), Random.Range and NextInt(min, max) take the range directly.

Shuffling and the seed. If the generator is seeded with an int, there are at most 2³² distinct sequences, and 13! already exceeds 2³². So even a fair Fisher–Yates cannot produce every permutation of a 52-card deck — most of them are unreachable. For a real-money card game that matters; for a Tetris bag it does not.

Pseudo-random distribution. “Fair” randomness in games often feels unfair: three misses in a row at a 50% chance are annoying. So the chance grows with each miss and resets on success: the average frequency stays the same, but long streaks disappear. The Tetris bag solves the same problem for ordering.
